`@noctcore/auth-nestjs` wires the core into a Nest app with the parts that are easy to get wrong done by default: every route needs a session unless it says otherwise, CSRF is checked before any guard, and the client IP behind a proxy cannot be left to chance. The core stays the same: the flows return `AuthResult` values and never throw HTTP errors, and the module only decides who gets through.

This guide builds on [A Node server with Redis and Prisma](/auth/build/node-server/): `auth.ts` and `config.ts` there are used as they are. A full app with its tests is in `examples/nestjs` in the repository.

```sh
bun add @noctcore/auth-nestjs @noctcore/auth @nestjs/common @nestjs/core @nestjs/platform-express
```

NestJS 11 and 12 are supported, on the Express platform, for HTTP controllers. GraphQL resolvers, WebSocket gateways and microservice handlers are not supported yet: the guard refuses them unless they are `@Public()`, so they never get through without a session check by accident. The package uses Nest's legacy decorators, so set `experimentalDecorators` in your `tsconfig.json`, as every Nest project already does.

## The module

<Code code={appModuleTs} lang="ts" title="src/app.module.ts" />

<Code code={mailModuleTs} lang="ts" title="src/mail.module.ts" />

`AuthModule.forRootAsync` (or `forRoot` with the options directly) does five things, and none of them can be switched off:

- provides the `createAuth` result under the `AUTH` token, for your controllers and services;
- registers `SessionGuard` as a global guard;
- applies `CsrfMiddleware` to every route;
- provides `SessionCookies`, which writes a new or ended session onto the response;
- calls `auth.flush()` in `beforeApplicationShutdown`, so mail sends still in flight finish before your own `onApplicationShutdown` hooks close the database and Redis connections. Nest runs it on `app.close()`, and on SIGTERM once `main.ts` calls `app.enableShutdownHooks()`. The wait is bounded by the module's `shutdownTimeout` option (10 seconds by default), so a mailer whose `send` never settles cannot keep the app from closing: after that long, whatever is still running is logged through your `logger` as `Background flush stopped waiting`, with the task labels, and abandoned.

The module is global, so feature modules get the guard, the decorators and `AUTH` without importing it again. Boot fails on a CSRF secret shorter than 32 bytes, an empty origin allowlist, a `crossSiteOrigins` entry that is not one exact origin, a hop count that is not a whole number from 0 to 16, a trusted proxy list with an entry that is not an address, a CIDR range or a preset, a range that trusts every address, or a `clientIpHeader` that is not a header name or comes with a hop count instead of a proxy list. It also fails on a route whose decorators contradict each other: `@Public()` (on the route or its controller) together with `@RequireRole()` or `@RequireFreshAuth()`, or `@RequireRole()` without the `roles` option. The error names each route. Both this check and `describeRoutes` see the handlers a controller inherits from a base class or a mixin, the way Nest routes them: an override in the subclass replaces the base handler.

## The guard order

Nest runs middleware before guards, and the module uses that order on every request:

1. **`CsrfMiddleware`** reads the session cookie through the core (`readSessionToken`, then `validateRequest`) and keeps the result for the rest of the request, so the session is validated once. On an unsafe method it runs the three checks from [CSRF](/auth/learn/csrf/): the `Origin` must be on `allowedOrigins` (or `crossSiteOrigins`), `Sec-Fetch-Site` must say `same-origin` whenever the browser sends it (or `cross-site` from an origin on `crossSiteOrigins`, for a desktop shell; see [Cookies and desktop shells](/auth/learn/cookies-and-desktop-shells/)), and the `X-CSRF-Token` header must match the `csrf` cookie and be signed for this session, or before sign-in for this browser's pre-session id. A refusal is answered by the middleware itself, with `403` and the body `{"error":{"code":"forbidden"}}`, whichever check failed. It never calls `next(err)`, so no exception filter can turn the refusal into a message that says more.
2. **`SessionGuard`** first refuses, with the same `403`, any unsafe request the middleware never saw. Which routes Nest hands to a middleware depends on its version and on the global prefix (Nest 11.0 to 11.2.7 and 12.0.0 to 12.1.2 skip the prefix root, such as `POST /api` under `setGlobalPrefix('api')`, and 11.0.0 also skips prefix-excluded routes), so the guard does not rely on that mapping: on those versions an unsafe request to such a route is refused even when it is legitimate, until you upgrade Nest. Then it refuses a route without a valid session with `401` and `{"error":{"code":"session_expired"}}`, unless the route or its controller carries `@Public()`. It loads the user from your user store on every request, so a deleted user is out at once.
3. **`@TwoFactorEnrollment()`**: under the two-factor plugin's `enforcement`, a session past the grace window is `enrollment-only` and reaches only a route marked `@TwoFactorEnrollment()` (on the route or its controller); anything else answers `403` and `{"error":{"code":"two_factor_enrollment_required"}}`. The standing is read from this request's validation, so it follows the policy without a new sign-in. See [Enforcement with a grace period](/auth/build/two-factor/#enforcement-with-a-grace-period).
4. **`@RequireRole()`** runs only after the session and the user are known. The module's `roles` function is called with the user just loaded, on every request, so a role taken away stops working on the next request. No role is ever copied into the cookie or the session.
5. **`@RequireFreshAuth()`** asks the core's `requireFreshAuth` whether the session's last password proof is within `freshAuthAge`. A route can pass a shorter `maxAge`, never a longer one.

`@Public()` lets a request through without a session, and skips steps 3 to 5, only on a route with no role or fresh-auth requirement. The guard still resolves a session the request carries, and its user, on a public route, so `@CurrentSession()` and `@CurrentUser()` name the caller when there is one: flows that refuse another account's session, such as an email verification link, rely on that. A store failure in the middleware or the guard is answered with a fixed `500` and logged by its error name only, so no message with a session key reaches your logs.

Safe methods (`GET`, `HEAD`, `OPTIONS`) skip the CSRF check, never the session check. On a safe request the middleware also hands out what the page needs for its next unsafe one: a pre-session id when the browser has neither a session nor an id, and a `csrf` cookie when the one it holds is missing or bound to something else. A session cookie the core refused for good is cleared on the same response (`clearsSessionCookie`); one another request may still be adopting from your own store is kept (see [Switching from your own sessions](/auth/build/store-adapter/#switching-from-your-own-sessions)).

`csrf.exempt` lists paths that skip the middleware entirely, such as a webhook that proves itself with a signature. Nothing is minted on an exempt path, and the guard still applies to it: mark the webhook route `@Public()` as well, and check its signature in the handler.


### Background polls

Every request that carries a session counts as activity and refreshes its last-active time, at most once per `touchInterval`. For requests the page makes on its own, such as a poll on a timer, pass `touch` a predicate that returns false, so an idle session still expires while only those arrive (see [Background polls](/auth/learn/sessions-and-expiry/#background-polls)):

```ts
AuthModule.forRoot({
  // ...
  touch: (request) => !(request.method === 'GET' && request.path === '/api/notifications/count'),
});
```

The predicate sees the method, the path (a global prefix included, no query string, and not normalised: a trailing slash or another case is a different path, so lower-case it and strip a trailing slash before comparing, or the poll touches) and the headers, and runs before the middleware validates the session. Under nestjs-trpc the tRPC context validates the same request again with its own `touch`, and a poll stays passive only when both say so (see [Use with tRPC](/auth/build/trpc/#background-polls)). It cannot read route decorators: the middleware validates the session before Nest picks a handler. A passive request is still answered with its session, and the CSRF checks and the guard's decisions do not change. `touch: false` touches on no request; the default, `true`, on every one.

## Signing in and out

<Code code={authControllerTs} lang="ts" title="src/auth.controller.ts" />

- **`@AuthMeta()`** is the request's `RequestMeta`: the client IP through the trusted hops, the user agent and the `Origin`. Pass it to every flow.
- **`SessionCookies.set`** writes the session cookie, the trusted-device cookie and a CSRF cookie bound to the new session, and returns the token for the response body. Every flow that issues a session goes through it: sign-in, re-authentication, a password change, revoking the other sessions, a verified address. Each one rotates the session, so each one needs a new CSRF token.
- **`SessionCookies.signOut`** revokes the session through `auth.logout`, clears its cookie and starts a fresh pre-session with its own token.
- **`@CurrentUser()` and `@CurrentSession()`** read what the guard resolved from the stored session. On a public route they are `null` when nobody is signed in. Nothing in the module reads a user id from a header or the body.

### Verification links

`verifyEmailLink` above is a `@Public()` POST. The guard still resolves the session on a public route, so `@CurrentSession()` is the caller's session when there is one and `null` otherwise; pass it as it is. A link for one account opened while signed in as another is then refused (`401`, `session_expired`) and stays usable for its owner. By default a link opened with no session is refused the same way; with `emailVerification.linkWithoutSession` on it verifies the address and signs nobody in.

Never verify on a GET or when the page loads: mail scanners fetch links in mail, and with `linkWithoutSession` on a fetch that reaches this route verifies the account. Put the token in the URL fragment (``urls.verifyEmail: (token) => `${origin}/verify#${token}` ``), show a Confirm button, and POST the token on the click. See [Email verification](/auth/learn/email-verification/) for the trade-off.

## Protected routes

<Code code={accountControllerTs} lang="ts" title="src/account.controller.ts" />

The sessions routes name each session by its public `handle`, which is what `sessions.revoke` takes; a store key never reaches the response. A handle that names none of the caller's sessions, another user's included, answers `{ revoked: false }`. See [Session handles](/auth/learn/sessions-and-expiry/#session-handles).

`@RequireRole('a', 'b')` accepts a user with either role. On a controller and a handler both, each list must be satisfied.

## The trust-proxy rule

<Code code={mainTs} lang="ts" title="src/main.ts" />

`TRUST_PROXY` is the number of reverse proxies in front of the app. `X-Forwarded-For` is written by the client up to the first proxy you run, so the module trusts exactly that many hops, counted from the right, the same rule as the core's `clientIp`. Trusting everything lets a client choose its own IP and its own rate-limit bucket; trusting nothing behind a proxy puts every client in one bucket, where one attacker blocks logins for everyone.

- `trustedHopsFromEnv(process.env)` reads it for the module. Unset is `0` in development and **refused in production**, so a deploy that forgot it fails at boot instead of quietly trusting the wrong hops. `true` is refused anywhere, and so is a count above 16 or anything that is neither a hop count nor a valid proxy list.
- `TRUST_PROXY` can also list the proxies by address: `loopback, 10.0.0.0/8` trusts the loopback range and that subnet, with `loopback`, `linklocal` and `uniquelocal` expanded to the ranges Express uses. Then `X-Forwarded-For` is read only when the socket address is inside the list, so a client that reaches the app directly cannot pose as a proxy. An unknown name or a malformed range is refused at boot.
- `configureTrustProxy(app, process.env)` sets Express's `trust proxy` to the same count or list, so `req.ip` in your own code agrees with what the flows see. The module itself never reads `req.ip`.
- `clientIpHeader: 'cf-connecting-ip'` (off by default) reads the client IP from a single-address header your edge sets. It needs `TRUST_PROXY` (or `trustedHops`) as a proxy list and is refused at boot with a hop count, which never checks the socket address. It is read only when the socket address is inside the list and the value is exactly one IP; otherwise `X-Forwarded-For` decides. The list must name the edge itself, or hops that accept traffic only from the edge: someone who can reach a listed internal load balancer directly can set the header. Name only a header your edge always overwrites. Express's `req.ip` does not read it. See [Trust proxy and client IPs](/auth/learn/trust-proxy-and-client-ips/).

## The compile test

<Code code={appTestTs} lang="ts" title="test/app.test.ts" />

Boot the whole `AppModule` in a test. A provider Nest cannot resolve fails there, in CI, instead of on the first deploy. `describeRoutes(app)` lists every controller route with the rule the guard will apply (public or not, its roles, fresh auth), so the test can pin the list of open routes: opening a new one shows up in the diff as a change to that list. `examples/nestjs` walks the unsafe routes too, after a page visit for the CSRF token, and runs the same app end to end on Redis and PostgreSQL.

## Before going live

- Serve over HTTPS and leave `session.cookie.secure` on. The CSRF cookies follow the session cookie: `__Host-csrf` and `__Host-presession` when it is `__Host-session`, with the `SameSite` that `session.cookie.sameSite` gives the request's `Origin`.
- Set `TRUST_PROXY` to the number of proxies you actually run, or to their addresses.
- Keep the CSRF secret separate from the auth secret; during a rollover, list the new one first and the old one after it. Each safe request replaces a token signed by the old secret with one under the new secret. A page that kept the old token in memory gets one `403` after another request replaced the cookie, and should read the token again (or retry once after a safe request). Remove the old secret once your clients have made a safe request since the deploy (keeping it for one session idle timeout covers every signed-in client); a client that has not gets one 403, and a new token on its next safe request.
- Fastify is not supported yet. The middleware and the cookies work on the raw Node request and response, but only Express is tested.
- If you use a global prefix, run Nest 11.2.8 or later (or 12.1.3 or later), so the middleware reaches the prefix root and excluded routes and the guard's safety net never has to refuse a legitimate request.
